content: 1. If the eyes are swollen and discharging pus, this may indicate a gonococcal eye infection. Administer a single dose of an appropriate antibiotic for eye infections as per protocol K12. 2. Educate the mother on how to properly treat the baby’s eyes, following guidance in K13. 3. Schedule a follow-up visit in 2 days. If there is no improvement or the condition worsens, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. 4. Assess and treat the mother and her partner for possible gonorrhea, as outlined in E8. 5. If the umbilicus is red or the surrounding skin is inflamed, this suggests a local umbilical infection. Teach the mother how to manage umbilical infections as per K13. 6. If there is no improvement in 2 days or the condition worsens, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. 7. If there are fewer than 10 pustules on the skin, this indicates a local skin infection. Teach the mother how to treat skin infections as per K13. 8. Schedule a follow-up in 2 days. If the pustules do not improve or worsen, refer the baby urgently to a hospital. 9. If the baby exhibits any danger signs, such as fast breathing (over 60 breaths per minute), slow or gasping breathing (less than 30 breaths per minute), severe chest in-drawing, poor feeding, grunting, seizures, abdominal distension, diffuse cyanosis, a heart rate consistently over 180 beats per minute, floppiness or stiffness, lack of spontaneous movement, or a temperature below 35.5°C that does not rise after rewarming, urgent hospital referral is required. 10. If the umbilicus is draining pus or there is redness and swelling extending to the surrounding skin, or if there are more than 10 pustules, bullae, or signs of skin swelling, redness, or hardness, this may indicate a serious illness. Administer the first dose of two intramuscular antibiotics as per K12 and refer the baby urgently to a hospital. 11. For birth injuries such as bruises or swelling on the buttocks, a swollen head, or abnormal leg positioning after breech delivery, explain to the parents that these conditions are not painful for the baby and will resolve within 1-2 weeks without special treatment. Advise against forcing the legs into a different position and handle any immobile limbs gently without pulling. 12. If there is a malformation, refer the baby for specialized treatment if available. Provide reassurance to the parents and advise on surgical correction at an appropriate age if necessary. 13. If the mother complains of nipple or breast pain, assess her breasts for signs of fissures, swelling, redness, or tenderness. Measure her temperature to rule out infection. 14. For nipple soreness or fissures, encourage the mother to continue breastfeeding and teach her correct positioning and attachment techniques as per K3. Reassess after 2 feeds or 1 day. If there is no improvement, teach her how to express milk from the affected breast and feed the baby by cup while continuing breastfeeding on the healthy side. 15. For breast engorgement, encourage frequent breastfeeding and teach correct positioning and attachment. Advise the mother to feed more frequently and reassess after 2 feeds or 1 day. If there is no improvement, teach her to express enough milk before feeding to relieve discomfort. 16. For mastitis, where part of the breast is painful, swollen, and red, and the mother has a fever over 38°C, encourage continued breastfeeding, teach correct positioning and attachment, and prescribe a 10-day course of cloxacillin as per F5. Reassess in 2 days, and if there is no improvement or the condition worsens, refer the mother to a hospital. 17. If the mother is HIV-infected, advise her to breastfeed on the healthy breast and express and discard milk from the affected breast until the fever resolves. If the pain is severe, administer paracetamol as per F4. 18. If the breasts are healthy with no swelling, redness, tenderness, or fissures, reassure the mother. 19. Ensure the room is warm (at least 25°C with no drafts) and keep the baby with the mother, either in her bed or within easy reach. If the baby is in a cot, ensure they are dressed, wrapped, and covered with a blanket, with their head covered by a hat. 20. Support exclusive breastfeeding on demand, day and night. Assess breastfeeding in every baby before discharge and assist the mother with positioning and attachment if needed. 21. Teach the mother how to care for the baby, including keeping the baby warm, providing cord care, and maintaining hygiene. If the mother is unable to care for the baby, provide care or teach a companion. 22. Wash hands before and after handling the baby. Ask the mother and companion to monitor the baby for signs of cold feet, breathing difficulty, or other abnormalities and alert healthcare staff if these occur. 23. If the baby’s feet are cold, teach the mother to provide skin-to-skin contact and reassess in 1 hour. If the feet remain cold, measure the baby’s temperature and rewarm as per K9. 24. If there is bleeding from the cord, check if the tie is loose and retie it. For other bleeding, assess the baby immediately. 25. If the baby has difficulty feeding, teach the mother replacement feeding and cup feeding as per K6. Advise feeding more frequently on demand, day and night, and stopping other foods, drinks, or bottle feeding. Reassess at the next feed or follow-up visit in 2 days. 26. Counsel the mother on the importance of exclusive breastfeeding during pregnancy and after birth. Explain that breast milk contains all the nutrients a baby needs, is easily digested, protects against infection, and supports development and bonding. 27. Help the mother initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth. Let the baby rest on the mother’s chest in skin-to-skin contact and assist with breastfeeding when the baby shows readiness, such as looking around, opening their mouth, or searching. 28. Teach the mother correct positioning and attachment for breastfeeding. Ensure the baby’s head and body are aligned, facing the breast, and close to the mother’s body. Support the baby’s whole body, not just the neck and shoulders. 29. If the baby does not feed within 1 hour, examine the baby. If healthy, leave the baby with the mother to try again later and reassess in 3 hours. 30. If the mother is ill and unable to breastfeed, help her express milk and feed the baby by cup. If breastfeeding is not possible, use donated heat-treated breast milk or commercial infant formula. 31. For small or preterm babies, provide additional care, including frequent breastfeeding every 2-3 hours, daily assessment of feeding, and ensuring warmth through skin-to-skin contact and extra blankets. 32. Do not bathe small babies; wash them as needed. If feeding difficulties persist for 3 days or weight loss exceeds 10% of birth weight, refer for breastfeeding counseling and management. 33. Teach the mother how to express breast milk directly into the baby’s mouth or use cup feeding if the baby is not sucking effectively. Determine the appropriate daily milk amount based on the baby’s age. 34. If the baby has jaundice, refer them for phototherapy. If the baby has breathing difficulty, assess them immediately. 35. Do not discharge the baby before they are 24 hours old. Ensure the mother is confident in caring for the baby and has no concerns before discharge.
